title: I Recorded the Shop Vac Hour the Landlord Denied

parts.text: I knocked at 11:47 p.m. because the shop vac had been screaming through my headboard for an hour. I am twenty-seven, receptionist, notes on everything. My upstairs neighbor, Kyle, was "renovating" without a permit, at night, in slides. The hallway smelled like sawdust and cheap beer. He opened the door with the vac still on. "What?" he yelled. I yelled back, "Lease says quiet hours at ten." He laughed and kicked the door most of the way shut. I recorded the decibel app on my phone against my ceiling, then against the hallway. 81, then 84. I emailed the landlord, Rhonda, with the clips. She replied at 7:03 a.m.: Kyle is improving the unit, be grateful. My ceiling had a new crack shaped like a lazy river. I photographed it next to a grocery receipt for scale, bananas $1.27. Rhonda said cracks are character. Kyle started at 5:40 a.m. the next day with a nail gun. I called the non-emergency line. The officer was kind and tired. Kyle told him I was sensitive. The officer looked at the time. "Quiet hours," he said. Kyle unplugged for twenty minutes. Then the vac came back. Rhonda texted me: if you keep calling cops you'll be the problem on the lease. I stared at that sentence. Then Kyle drilled through his floor into my closet, a neat hole, daylight, and a screw dropped onto my winter coats.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: A screw is on my coat pile, Rhonda called me the problem, and the vac is still running.

social.video_title: He shop-vac'd through quiet hours into my closet — Part 1/2
social.description: Sawdust hallway, banana-receipt scale, and a landlord who called renovation gratitude. Then a screw hit my winter coats. Would you have called non-emergency?

parts.text: I bagged the screw and the coats and took a video of the hole. I sent it to Rhonda, to the city's housing email, and to my renter's insurance, which felt adult and unhinged. Kyle knocked, suddenly polite. "I'll patch it," he said. I said, "You'll patch it with a licensed person, not at midnight." Rhonda arrived that afternoon in a perfume that fought the sawdust and lost. She saw the hole and still said I was escalating. The city inspector did not say that. Kyle got a stop-work. Rhonda offered me one month free to "let it go." I asked for the hole, the quiet hours in writing, and the crack. She gave two of three. I moved at lease end anyway. Kyle's unit sat half-gutted. The new place has a neighbor who vacuums at noon like a citizen. I still flinch at shop vacs in hardware stores. I bought new coats. The screw sits in a jar on my bookshelf, which is a weird souvenir, and it keeps me from texting Rhonda on bad days. Quiet hours are a sentence in a PDF until they are a hole in a closet. I prefer the PDF, enforced. The cheap light over the sink flickered twice like punctuation I did not ask for.

social.video_title: The inspector believed the hole more than gratitude — Part 2/2
social.description: A bagged screw, a stop-work sticker, and one month free I did not treat as a personality. Would you have moved anyway?
